stages.title: Intermediate vocabulary
stages.hook: If you want to find a pharmacy in a Portuguese-speaking town, which words do you need?
explain: Town vocabulary: cidade (city), rua (street), praça (square), ponte (bridge), mercado (market), hospital, biblioteca (library), farmácia (pharmacy), banco (bank), correio (post office). Many words are similar to Spanish and English because of Latin roots: biblioteca, hospital, farmácia.

Location words: perto de (near), longe de (far from), ao lado de (next to), em frente a (opposite), entre (between). 'A farmácia fica ao lado do banco' means 'The pharmacy is next to the bank'. Note the contraction de + o = do and a + o = ao. Some words differ across the Portuguese-speaking world: rua in Brazil and Portugal, but 'avenida' is used for big streets in all countries.
stages.mnemonic: Perto, longe, ao lado: where is the farmácia?
sentences: The pharmacy is next to the bank.
The library is near the square.
The market is far from here.

gq.why: Ao lado de means next to.

panel.q: Why is it 'ao lado do banco'?
Which sentence correctly says 'near the square'?
Why are many town words similar in Portuguese, Spanish and English?

teach.model: Use perto de, longe de, ao lado de, em frente a. Prepositions contract with articles: de + o = do, de + a = da.

points.ask: How do I say where something is?
What happens with de and o?

trip.prompt: Find town words and their English relatives.

stages.title: Verb forms and time expressions
stages.hook: How do you say 'I spoke', 'I was speaking' and 'I will speak'?
explain: The simple past (pretérito perfeito) is for completed actions: falei, comi, parti (I spoke, I ate, I left). The imperfect (imperfeito) is for habits and background in the past: falava, comia, partia. Compare: 'Ontem comi arroz' (Yesterday I ate rice) and 'Quando era criança, comia arroz todos os dias' (When I was a child, I ate rice every day).

Future: in everyday speech use ir + infinitive: 'Vou falar' (I am going to speak). Time words: ontem (yesterday), hoje, amanhã, agora, antes, depois, já (already), ainda (still, yet), sempre (always), nunca (never), às vezes (sometimes). In Brazil 'estou falando' (I am speaking), in Portugal 'estou a falar'. The verbs ser and ir share the past: fui, foi, fomos, foram.
stages.mnemonic: Falei is finished; falava is a film in the background.
items: I was eating / used to eat
sentences: I am going to speak tomorrow.
She never goes to the beach.

gq.q: Which form is the simple past of 'comer' (eu)?
How does Portugal say 'I am speaking'?

panel.q: Why is 'Quando era criança, comia arroz' imperfect?
o: It is a single completed act
It describes a habit in the past
panel.why: The imperfect describes habits and background.

panel.q: What is special about 'fui'?
o: It is the past of both ser and ir
panel.why: Fui = I was or I went.

panel.q: Which time word means 'still / yet'?

teach.model: Perfect past for completed actions, imperfect for habits. Future with vou + infinitive. Time words: ontem, hoje, amanhã, já, ainda, sempre, nunca.

points.ask: How do I say the future?

stages.title: Complex sentence introduction
stages.hook: How can you join two sentences with 'because', 'when' and 'if'?
explain: Connectors build longer sentences: porque (because), quando (when), se (if), mas (but), que (that), enquanto (while), depois que (after). Examples: 'Fiquei em casa porque estava chovendo' (I stayed home because it was raining). 'Quando chego, ligo para você' (When I arrive, I call you).

For 'if' about the future, Portuguese uses the future subjunctive: 'Se chover, fico em casa' (If it rains, I stay home). 'Embora' (although) takes the subjunctive: 'Embora esteja cansado, vou à festa.' The word 'que' joins a reported idea: 'Eu sei que ele chegou' (I know that he arrived). In Brazil and Portugal people say 'Penso que' and 'Acho que' for I think that.
stages.mnemonic: Porque gives a reason; quando gives time; se gives a condition.
sentences: I stayed home because it rained.
If it rains, I stay home.

panel.q: Why is it 'Se chover' and not 'Se chove'?
o: The future subjunctive is used after se for open future conditions
panel.why: Portuguese uses the future subjunctive here.

panel.q: Which phrase is correct?
What does 'por isso' do?

teach.model: Use porque (reason), quando (time), se (condition), mas (contrast), embora (concession). Se + future subjunctive: Se chover...

points.ask: How do I give a reason?

stages.title: Reading short stories
stages.hook: How does a Portuguese fable begin, and who wins the race between the cicada and the ant?
explain: Stories often begin 'Era uma vez ...' (Once upon a time ...). They use the imperfect for description and the perfect for events: 'Era uma vez uma cigarra que cantava todo o verão. Uma formiga trabalhava sem parar. Quando o inverno chegou, a cigarra não tinha comida.' Connectors: então (then), de repente (suddenly), por fim (finally).

Famous Lusophone writers include Machado de Assis (Brazil), Eça de Queirós (Portugal), Mia Couto (Mozambique) and José Eduardo Agualusa (Angola). When reading a short story, ask: who (personagem), where (lugar), what happens (enredo), and what lesson (moral).
stages.mnemonic: Era uma vez: imperfect for the scene, perfect for the events.
sentences: Once upon a time there was a girl.

gq.q: Which phrase opens a fairy tale?
gq.why: Era uma vez means once upon a time.

panel.q: Why use the imperfect in 'a cigarra cantava'?
o: It describes an ongoing background action

panel.q: Which word signals a sudden event?
What is 'enredo'?

teach.model: Begin with Era uma vez. Use the imperfect for scene and background and the perfect for events. Look for personagem, enredo, moral.

stages.title: Listening comprehension
stages.hook: If an announcement says 'O voo para Lisboa parte às quinze horas', when does the flight leave?
explain: Listening practice often includes numbers, times and places. 'O voo parte às quinze horas' means the flight leaves at 3 pm (15:00). Official time often uses the 24-hour clock. Key words: voo (flight), portão (gate), atraso (delay), chegada (arrival), partida (departure).

Spoken Brazilian Portuguese shortens words: 'tá' for está, 'pra' for para, 'né' for não é, 'cê' for você. In Portugal, unstressed vowels are weakened and some words sound like they are missing vowels. Listen first for the main idea, then for details. If you miss it, say 'Pode repetir?'
stages.mnemonic: Listen for who, what, where, when.

gq.q: What does 'pra' stand for in speech?

panel.q: Why do announcements use the 24-hour clock?
o: To avoid confusion between morning and afternoon

panel.q: What is the best first step in listening?
Which word is the written form of 'tá'?

teach.model: Listen for numbers, places and times. Spoken Brazilian Portuguese shortens words: tá, pra, né, cê. Ask Pode repetir? if you miss it.

trip.prompt: Try listening to an airport announcement.

stages.title: Conversation and pronunciation
stages.hook: Why do 'leite' and 'dia' sound different in São Paulo and Lisbon?
explain: Pronunciation differs across the Portuguese-speaking world. In many Brazilian accents, t and d before i or final e sound like ch and j: dia sounds like 'jia', leite like 'leitchi'. In Portugal, unstressed vowels are shortened or almost silent: 'telefone' sounds close to 'tlfon'.

The letter r also varies: at the start of a word or rr it is a breathy h in much of Brazil (rua, carro), but a rolled or uvular sound in Portugal. Final s sounds like sh in Rio de Janeiro and in Portugal, and like s in São Paulo. All varieties share nasal vowels. Practise by imitating audio.
stages.mnemonic: Brazil opens vowels; Portugal closes them.

o: Like dee-ah with a hard d always
gq.why: D before i often sounds like j.

gq.q: What happens to unstressed vowels in Portugal?

panel.q: Which letter combination is often a breathy h in Brazil?
Why can two speakers say 'telefone' differently?
What is the best way to practise?

teach.model: Brazilian t and d before i sound like ch and j. European Portuguese reduces unstressed vowels. R varies by region. Nasal vowels are common.

stages.title: Writing paragraphs
stages.hook: How do you organise a short paragraph about your weekend in Portuguese?
explain: A paragraph has a topic sentence, details and a conclusion. Use sequence words: primeiro (first), depois (then), em seguida (next), finalmente (finally), por isso (so), porém (however), além disso (in addition). Example: 'No sábado acordei cedo. Primeiro tomei café da manhã. Depois fui à praia. Finalmente voltei para casa.'

Check agreement: o/a, um/uma, adjectives, and verb endings. Use the perfect for events and the imperfect for background. Start each sentence with a capital letter and end with a full stop. Remember the accent marks: está, você, também.
stages.mnemonic: Primeiro, depois, finalmente: three steps make a paragraph.
sentences: On Saturday I woke up early.

gq.q: Which tense is natural for events on Saturday?

panel.q: Why check accent marks?
panel.why: Accent marks are part of spelling.

panel.q: Which linking word adds information?
Which sentence has agreement?

teach.model: Plan topic, details, conclusion. Link with primeiro, depois, em seguida, finalmente. Check agreement and accents.

stages.title: Cultural expressions and idioms
stages.hook: What do Brazilians say instead of 'cool', and what do Portuguese people say?
explain: Everyday expressions differ by country. 'Legal' (Brazil) and 'fixe' (Portugal) mean cool. 'Beleza!' is a common Brazilian reply meaning great or OK. 'Valeu!' is Brazilian slang for thanks. 'Giro' in Portugal means nice or cute. 'Saudade' has no exact English translation.

Polite expressions: 'Bom apetite' (enjoy your meal), 'Saúde!' (cheers, or bless you), 'Parabéns!' (congratulations), 'Boa sorte' (good luck), 'Fica à vontade' (make yourself at home), 'Até já' (see you soon in Portugal). Do not translate idioms word for word.
stages.mnemonic: Legal in Brazil, fixe in Portugal.

panel.q: Why is 'legal' tricky for learners?
o: It also means lawful, but in speech means cool in Brazil

panel.q: Which phrase do you say before a meal?
Why not translate idioms literally?
o: Their meaning is not the sum of their words

teach.model: Brazil: legal, beleza, valeu. Portugal: fixe, giro. Polite phrases: bom apetite, saúde, parabéns, boa sorte.

trip.prompt: Find differences between Brazilian and European slang.

stages.title: Practical travel communication
stages.hook: You need to buy a ticket to São Paulo. What do you say?
explain: Travel phrases: 'Uma passagem para São Paulo, por favor' (Brazil) or 'Um bilhete para São Paulo' (Portugal). 'Onde fica o hotel?' (Where is the hotel?), 'Vire à direita' (Turn right), 'Vire à esquerda' (Turn left), 'Siga em frente' (Go straight ahead). Transport words differ: ônibus and trem in Brazil; autocarro and comboio in Portugal.

At the hotel: 'Tenho uma reserva em nome de ...' (I have a reservation in the name of ...), 'Quanto custa o quarto?' (How much is the room?). At the airport: passaporte, bagagem (luggage), embarque (boarding). Ask for help politely: 'Pode me ajudar?' (Brazil) or 'Pode ajudar-me?' (Portugal).
stages.mnemonic: Passagem or bilhete, ônibus or autocarro: same trip, two vocabularies.
sentences: One ticket to São Paulo, please.

panel.q: How would a Portuguese traveller say 'bus'?
Why does 'Pode me ajudar?' differ from 'Pode ajudar-me?'
o: Brazil and Portugal place the pronoun differently
panel.why: Pronoun placement is a regional feature.

panel.q: Which request is polite?
panel.why: The question with por favor is polite.

teach.model: Ask for passagem (Brazil) or bilhete (Portugal). Use Vire à direita, Siga em frente. Pronoun placement differs: me ajudar / ajudar-me.

points.ask: How do I ask for help?
